title: Cross-tenant branch read in check-in access-scope resolver via unscoped findUnique with client-supplied branch_id
evidence: targetBranchId is client-controlled: `const targetBranchId = ctx.request.branch_id ?? ctx.membership.branch_id ?? ctx.member.branch_id;` (line 34-37, ctx.request.branch_id is the raw request value). It is then read UNSCOPED in resolveAllAccess: `const target = await ctx.prisma.branch.findUnique({ where: { id: targetBranchId }, select: { organization_id: true } });` (line 144-147) and in resolveCityAccess: `const target = await ctx.prisma.branch.findUnique({ where: { id: targetBranchId }, select: { city: true } });` (line 202-205). The $use middleware guard for findUnique (prisma.service.ts:155) only fires `if (result && (result as any).gym_id && (result as any).gym_id !== gymId)` — but the `select` here omits gym_id, so result.gym_id is undefined and the cross-tenant guard is skipped. The orchestrator's own gym-scoped branch load (`branch.findFirst({ where: { id: input.branch_id, gym_id: gymId } })`, check-in.orchestrator.ts:157-158) returns null for a foreign branch, and branchForCtx falls back to the member's own branch (line 173) WITHOUT rejecting the foreign id, which is preserved verbatim in ctx.request.branch_id (line 234).
impact: A member of gym A on an all_access or city_access plan can submit a check-in with branch_id belonging to gym B; the resolver reads gym B's branch row (organization_id / city) with no gym scoping — a cross-tenant read. For city_access, if gym B has a branch in the plan's allowed_city the resolver returns allowed:true, granting a check-in access decision computed from another tenant's data.
fix: Do not use findUnique here. Load the target branch gym-scoped like the orchestrator already does: `ctx.prisma.branch.findFirst({ where: { id: targetBranchId, gym_id: ctx.gym_id }, select: {...} })`, and treat a null result as branch_not_found. Reuse the already-gym-scoped ctx.branch instead of re-fetching by the raw request id.

verdict.reasoning: Independently reproduced from the real code. (1) targetBranchId is client-controlled: access-scope.resolver.ts:34-37 sets it from ctx.request.branch_id, which the orchestrator populates verbatim from raw input.branch_id (check-in.orchestrator.ts:234) — the gym-scoped branch load (line 157-158) returns null for a foreign branch and branchForCtx silently falls back to the member's own branch (line 173) without rejecting the foreign id. (2) resolveAllAccess (line 144-147) and resolveCityAccess (line 201-204) both call ctx.prisma.branch.findUnique({ where: { id: targetBranchId }, select: { organization_id: true } / { city: true } }) with no gym_id filter and gym_id omitted from select. (3) Branch IS a tenant model (tenant-models.ts:17), so the $use middleware runs, but the findUnique guard (prisma.service.ts:155) is `if (result && (result as any).gym_id && ...)` — since gym_id is not in the select, result.gym_id is undefined and the cross-tenant guard is skipped, returning the foreign gym's branch row. (4) The path is reachable via BranchAccessRule (order 10) for all_access/city_access plans. The city_access branch reaches the unscoped read whenever the member's home-branch city differs from the plan's allowed city (the normal cross-branch case); the all_access branch can short-circuit at line 138 when the member's own branch org matches the plan org, but still reaches the read when planOrg is null or differs. This is a genuine app-layer tenant-isolation bypass of the exact R3 findUnique-fails-open class. I adjust severity to medium rather than high: the leaked data is narrow (a branch's organization_id/city), the attacker must already possess an unguessable foreign branch UUID, and the resulting access decision is only 'overridable' and records the check-in under the member's own gym_id — a real but limited blast radius.

title: $use findUnique cross-tenant post-check fails open whenever a select/include omits gym_id
evidence: findUnique/findUniqueOrThrow are not where-injected; they rely on a result post-check: `const result = await next(params); if (result && (result as any).gym_id && (result as any).gym_id !== gymId) { ...return null }` (lines 154-164). The guard is gated on `(result as any).gym_id` being truthy, so any findUnique that passes a `select` or `include` which does not include gym_id yields result.gym_id === undefined and the cross-tenant check never runs — the foreign row is returned. Confirmed reachable at access-scope.resolver.ts:144/202 (above) and check-in.orchestrator.ts:338 `member.findUnique({ where: { id: stc.mid }, select: { id: true, qr_version: true } })` (the latter is mitigated by the signed `verified.payload.sid !== gymId` check at line 332, but the isolation layer itself provides no protection).
impact: Systemic fails-open in the crown-jewel isolation layer: any current or future findUnique on a tenant model that projects columns without gym_id silently bypasses tenant isolation and can return another gym's row when the id is attacker-influenced. This is the R3 'findUnique fails-open' leak class, only partially closed.
fix: Make the post-check fail closed: always force gym_id into the findUnique select (merge `select: { ...userSelect, gym_id: true }`), then strip it from the returned object after verifying it equals the context gym_id; or convert findUnique on tenant models to a gym-scoped findFirst (where: { <unique>, gym_id }). Treat a missing gym_id on the fetched row as a violation, not a pass.

verdict.reasoning:
I independently verified the defect by reading the actual code.

CORE CLAIM CONFIRMED (prisma.service.ts:152-165): The $use findUnique/findUniqueOrThrow branch does NOT where-inject gym_id; it relies on a post-fetch check `if (result && (result as any).gym_id && (result as any).gym_id !== gymId)`. The guard is gated on `(result as any).gym_id` being truthy. When a caller passes a `select` that omits gym_id, `result.gym_id` is `undefined`, the `&&` short-circuits, and the cross-tenant comparison never runs — the row is returned regardless of tenant. This is a genuine fail-open.

The finding is actually STRONGER than reported: the identical fails-open pattern exists in the second isolation layer, the extension client, at tenant-prisma.extension.ts:106-113 (findUnique) and 128-136 (findUniqueOrThrow) — same `(result as any).gym_id &&` gate. So BOTH isolation layers share the defect; there is no compensating layer.

REACHABILITY CONFIRMED with a real, unmitigated select-projecting call site: wallet.service.ts:34 `this.tenant.client.member.findUnique({ where: { id: memberId }, select: { id: true } })`. gym_id is not selected, so neither the $use nor the extension post-check fires; a foreign member id yields a truthy `{id}` and the existence check at line 38 passes for another gym's member.

NUANCE (does not refute): `include`-based findUnique (e.g. plans.service.ts:101) is NOT vulnerable because Prisma `include` returns all top-level scalars, so gym_id is present and the check works — only `select` that omits gym_id triggers the fail-open. The check-in.orchestrator.ts:338 site cited (select: {id, qr_version}) IS a vulnerable select, but as the finding itself notes it is independently mitigated by the signed `verified.payload.sid !== gymId` check at line 332. The isolation layer still provides no protection there — the mitigation is external.

The evidence was read accurately, the path is reachable, no compensating control exists in the isolation layer itself, and the systemic fail-open in the crown-jewel tenant-isolation layer is real (the R3 leak class).

title: JwtAuthGuard fails open to full 'owner' privileges when JWT metadata omits role or RBAC returns no rows
evidence: let role = metadata.role || 'owner';  ... (line 97) if (studioId) { ... if (userRoles.length > 0) { role = primaryRole.role_name; ... } } ... (line 137) if (Object.keys(permissions).length === 0) { permissions = metadata.permissions || DEFAULT_ROLE_PERMISSIONS[role] || {}; }
impact: Any admin-side token whose Supabase user_metadata lacks `role` (or where getUserRoles/resolvePermissions returns nothing for the studio) is assigned role='owner' and DEFAULT_ROLE_PERMISSIONS['owner'] (full CRUD+export on members/payments/staff/settings/roles/inventory — default-permissions.ts:25). Because both RolesGuard (roles.guard.ts:44-48 owner/brand_owner/super_admin bypass) and PermissionsGuard (permissions.guard.ts:41 ADMIN_ROLES bypass) short-circuit on role='owner', every @Roles/@Permissions gate is bypassed, and StripSecretsInterceptor (strip-secrets.interceptor.ts:55) treats them as owner so salary/base_salary/hourly_rate are NOT stripped. studio_id/role/branch_ids are all read from client-influenceable user_metadata and are never cross-checked against DB membership on this path, so this is a fail-open privilege escalation rather than a deny.
fix: Default `role` to a deny/least-privilege value (or reject) instead of 'owner'; when studioId is present require at least one RBAC role row before granting any permissions; never fall back to DEFAULT_ROLE_PERMISSIONS['owner'] or to client-supplied metadata.permissions for authorization.

verdict.reasoning: All cited lines verified verbatim. jwt-auth.guard.ts:91 defaults `role` to 'owner' when `metadata.role` is absent. The RBAC override (lines 97-129) only fires when studioId is present AND userRoles.length > 0; on the empty/throw path role and permissions are never recomputed. Lines 137-138 then grant DEFAULT_ROLE_PERMISSIONS['owner'] (full CRUD+export, confirmed in default-permissions.ts:25-39) or client-supplied metadata.permissions. Both RolesGuard (roles.guard.ts:45-48) and PermissionsGuard (permissions.guard.ts:14,41) bypass all gates for role='owner', and StripSecretsInterceptor (strip-secrets.interceptor.ts:26,55) treats owner as privileged so salary/base_salary/hourly_rate are not stripped. studio_id/role/branch_ids come solely from user_metadata (lines 87-93) with no DB-membership cross-check when RBAC returns no rows — a fail-open grant, not a deny. Reachability is real: the DEFAULT_ROLE_PERMISSIONS comment documents the RBAC-not-seeded state as expected, and Supabase user_metadata is user-writable via GoTrue updateUser, so an authenticated user can set studio_id to a gym where they hold no RBAC assignment (getUserRoles → 0 rows) with role omitted, landing on owner with full permissions over another tenant's data. I could not refute the finding; the evidence was read correctly and the defect reproduces from source. Severity kept at high (not critical) only because full weaponization depends on Supabase's client-writable-metadata default, which is standard but not provable from this repo alone; the defensive fail-open-to-owner default is itself an unambiguous, reportable authorization defect regardless.

title: RBAC resolution errors are swallowed and downgrade to trusting client-supplied metadata (fail-open on infra failure)
evidence: } catch (error) { this.logger.warn(`RBAC resolution failed for user ${user.id} in studio ${studioId}`, ...); // Fall through to legacy resolution below }  ... permissions = metadata.permissions || DEFAULT_ROLE_PERMISSIONS[role] || {};
impact: A transient failure in rbacService.getUserRoles/resolvePermissions (DB hiccup, query error) is caught and the request proceeds using role/permissions derived from the client-controlled JWT metadata and DEFAULT_ROLE_PERMISSIONS. During any RBAC/DB disruption, authorization silently degrades to trusting metadata (which, with the role default of 'owner', yields owner access). Authorization should fail closed, not open, on infrastructure errors.
fix: On RBAC resolution error, reject the request (throw) or grant an explicit no-permission context; do not fall through to metadata/default-permission authorization when the authoritative RBAC lookup failed.

verdict.reasoning: Verified directly in backend/src/common/guards/jwt-auth.guard.ts. The catch at line 130-133 swallows any error from the authoritative RBAC lookups (rbacService.getUserRoles / resolvePermissions) with only a logger.warn and an explicit "Fall through to legacy resolution below" comment — no re-throw. On that error path `permissions` is still `{}`, so line 137's `if (Object.keys(permissions).length === 0)` is entered and authorization is rebuilt from client-influenced data: `permissions = metadata.permissions || DEFAULT_ROLE_PERMISSIONS[role]`, where `role = metadata.role || 'owner'` (line 91). Execution then reaches `return true` (line 178). The metadata comes from `user.user_metadata` (lines 62/68/74), which in Supabase is self-updatable by the authenticated user (unlike app_metadata) and re-signed into the JWT, so it is not authoritative. No mitigating fail-closed control exists for RBAC resolution failure — the only throws cover missing header/invalid token/missing DB user. Thus a transient DB/RBAC fault silently degrades authorization to trusting metadata, with a default of 'owner'. The defect is reproduced from real code. Nuance: the same metadata fallback (line 137) also runs in the non-error case when userRoles is empty (legacy path), so it is not purely error-handling; but the reported defect — errors swallowed and downgrading to metadata/default-permission authorization instead of failing closed — is accurate. Medium is appropriate since exploitation requires an infra fault or reliance on self-updatable user_metadata, but the 'owner' default amplifies impact.

title: Member refresh-token rotation lacks reuse/family revocation on a revoked-token replay
evidence: if (!row || row.revoked_at || row.expires_at.getTime() < Date.now()) { throw MemberException.invalidToken('Refresh token is invalid or expired.'); }
impact: Presenting an already-rotated (revoked) member refresh token just returns 401; it does not detect token theft or revoke the currently-active token in the chain. If an attacker exfiltrates a refresh token and rotates it before the legitimate client, the attacker holds a valid session and the victim's failed refresh is the only (silent) signal — the compromised chain is never force-revoked.
fix: On presentation of a token whose row is already revoked, treat it as reuse: revoke the entire replaced_by chain / all active refresh tokens for that app_user and require re-authentication.

verdict.reasoning: Independently reproduced from real code. In refresh() (member-auth.service.ts:193-227), a revoked/expired/missing token row hits line 198 and throws a generic invalidToken 401. On rotation, line 224 writes revoked_at + replaced_by, building a chain — but a grep across all of backend/src/member confirms replaced_by is never read anywhere (only written at line 224 and asserted in the spec). There is no reuse-detection or family/chain revocation: revokeAll/revokeFamily do not exist. So replaying an already-rotated (revoked) refresh token simply returns 401 without revoking the currently-active token in the chain or all active tokens for the app_user. This matches the finding exactly: in a token-theft scenario the compromised chain is never force-invalidated and the victim's failed refresh is the only silent signal. This is a real defense-in-depth gap versus the OAuth 2.0 Security BCP rotation-with-reuse-detection pattern. It is not an active auth bypass (revoked tokens are still correctly rejected), so low severity is appropriate.

title: SSRF: tenant-configured webhook URL is fetched server-side with no private-IP/host allowlist, and the response body is stored and readable
evidence: URL comes straight from tenant input with only `@IsUrl({ require_tld: false })` (backend/src/platform/dto/webhook.dto.ts:17) — which explicitly permits schemeless-TLD hosts like `localhost`/`169.254.169.254`. It is then fetched verbatim: `const response = await fetch(webhook.url, { method: 'POST', ... body, signal: controller.signal });` and the reply is persisted: `response_body: responseBody.substring(0, 1000)` (line 249). The same sink exists in the queue path: backend/src/queue/processors/webhook.processor.ts:58 (`await fetch(webhook.url, ...)`) with `response_body: responseBody.substring(0, 1000)` (line 79).
impact: An authenticated gym owner (Roles('owner')) can register a webhook pointing at internal services or the cloud metadata endpoint (e.g. http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/, http://localhost:port). On any matching event the prod backend (deployed on a VPS per project notes) issues the request from inside the network, and up to 1000 chars of the response are saved to WebhookDelivery.response_body — retrievable via GET /api/v1/webhooks/:id/deliveries. This is SSRF with response exfiltration reachable from a customer role.
fix: Before fetching, resolve the URL host and reject non-public targets: block loopback/link-local/private CIDRs (127.0.0.0/8, 10/8, 172.16/12, 192.168/16, 169.254/16, ::1, fc00::/7) and metadata IPs, enforce https + allowed ports, and re-validate after DNS resolution (guard against DNS-rebinding). Consider an egress proxy/allowlist for outbound webhook delivery.

verdict.reasoning:
The code-level defect is real and accurately quoted: webhooks.service.ts:228 (and the duplicate at webhook.processor.ts:58) fetch a tenant-controlled URL verbatim with no private-IP/host allowlist, DNS-rebinding guard, or scheme/port enforcement; the DTO only applies @IsUrl({require_tld:false}) (webhook.dto.ts:17), which permits localhost and IP literals like 169.254.169.254; and up to 1000 chars of the response are persisted (response_body, line 249/79) and are readable via getDeliveries() → GET /api/v1/webhooks/:id/deliveries. Webhook creation is gated to @Roles('owner'). All of that is confirmed by reading the files.

However, the finding's core reachability claim — "on any matching event the prod backend issues the request" — is NOT reproducible in the current code. The private fetch method dispatchDelivery() is only called from dispatch() and retryDelivery(). Grepping WebhooksService across backend/src returns only the DI registration (platform.module.ts) and the controller; dispatch() is invoked by no other module and no endpoint, so no domain event ever triggers a delivery. enqueueWebhook() (queue.service.ts:93) has zero callers, so the BullMQ processor path is dead as well. The one HTTP-reachable trigger, retryDelivery(), requires a pre-existing WebhookDelivery row, but deliveries are only created inside the (dormant) dispatch/processor paths and there is no other creation route — so retryDelivery always throws NotFound. Net: the outbound-webhook feature is half-wired; the SSRF sink genuinely lacks any guard but has no reachable trigger today. It is a real latent vulnerability that would become live the instant event wiring is added (a public dispatch(), 20 enumerated events, and a BullMQ processor all exist and clearly intend that), but it is not currently exploitable as an active SSRF from a customer role. Because the sink defect is unambiguously real yet the stated exploit path is presently unreachable, the honest verdict is UNCERTAIN with a downgraded severity.

title: Member photo signed URLs are minted with a 1-year expiry, violating the 1-hour private-bucket policy
evidence: `.createSignedUrl(fileName, 365 * 24 * 60 * 60);` with the comment `// Generate signed URL (1 year expiry for profile photos)` on a private bucket (`member-photos`, created with `public: false`).
impact: CLAUDE.md/security rules require serving private Storage via 1-hour signed URLs. A 365-day signed URL is effectively a permanent unauthenticated link to member PII (photos). If it leaks via logs, HTTP referer, browser history, cache, or a shared link, it grants a full year of access with no revocation short of deleting/rotating the object.
fix: Reduce the signed-URL TTL to ~1 hour and generate on-demand when the photo is displayed rather than returning a long-lived link at upload time.

verdict.reasoning: Verified directly in backend/src/uploads/uploads.controller.ts. The `member-photos` bucket is created with `public: false` (line 53), and line 74 mints the signed URL with `createSignedUrl(fileName, 365 * 24 * 60 * 60)` — a 365-day (1-year) TTL, with the confirming comment on line 71 "1 year expiry for profile photos". This is 3650x the 1-hour signed-URL ceiling mandated by CLAUDE.md's security rules ("Supabase Storage buckets are private; serve via 1-hour signed URLs"). The endpoint POST api/v1/uploads/photo is a live, JwtAuthGuard-protected handler that returns the long-lived URL to the caller, and files are keyed under studio_id, so the object is member/staff photo PII. Refutation attempts fail: this is the only place the URL is minted (no shorter-TTL control elsewhere), the bucket is genuinely private (not public where TTL would be moot), and the arithmetic is unambiguous. Severity medium is appropriate rather than high/critical because it is not a cross-tenant leak or auth bypass — exploitation requires the bearer URL to leak (logs, HTTP referer, browser history/cache, shared link), after which it grants ~1 year of unauthenticated access with no revocation short of rotating/deleting the object.

title: Upload validation trusts client-supplied MIME and never validates extension or file content
evidence: fileFilter only inspects the client-set header: `if (!file.mimetype.startsWith('image/')) { return cb(new BadRequestException('Only image files are allowed'), false); }`. The stored key's extension is taken verbatim from the attacker-controlled filename: `const ext = file.originalname.split('.').pop() || 'jpg';` then `` const fileName = `${user.studio_id}/${randomUUID()}.${ext}`; ``. No magic-byte/content sniffing, no extension allowlist. The logo endpoint (line 100+) additionally allows `image/svg+xml` into a PUBLIC bucket and returns getPublicUrl().
impact: multipart `Content-Type` is fully client-controlled, so the `image/` gate is trivially spoofed — a non-image (or a script-bearing SVG for the public logo bucket) can be stored, and the object key extension can be arbitrary. Project rules mandate server-side MIME + size + extension validation; extension and real content type are not validated. SVGs served from the public studio-assets bucket can carry inline script (stored-XSS risk if rendered inline).
fix: Validate against an explicit extension allowlist, verify actual content type from magic bytes (e.g. file-type sniffing) not the client header, and drop/normalize the stored extension. For the public logo bucket, either disallow SVG or sanitize it and serve with Content-Disposition/`image/svg+xml` hardening.

verdict.reasoning: Verified directly against backend/src/uploads/uploads.controller.ts. Line 33/94: fileFilter checks only `file.mimetype.startsWith('image/')`, which is multer's parse of the client-supplied multipart Content-Type header — trivially spoofable. Line 45/103: the stored object extension is taken verbatim from the attacker-controlled `file.originalname` with no allowlist. There is no magic-byte/content sniffing anywhere. The Supabase bucket `allowedMimeTypes` (line 55/113) is not a real second layer because the upload passes `contentType: file.mimetype` (line 62/119) — the same spoofable client value — so non-image bytes declared as `image/png` are storable. Line 113 additionally allows `image/svg+xml` into a `public: true` bucket returned via `getPublicUrl` (line 129-131). Both endpoints are reachable by any authenticated user (JwtAuthGuard). This directly violates the project's own stated requirement to validate uploads server-side by MIME + size + extension. Two mitigating factors keep this at medium rather than high: the member-photos bucket is private (signed URLs), and public SVGs are served from the Supabase storage domain rather than the app origin, so inline-SVG script does not execute in the app's origin/cookie context. The evidence quotes match the real code exactly; the defect reproduces independently.

title: Committed default super-admin password in tracked saas-control-center/.env.example
evidence: `SUPER_ADMIN_PASSWORD="MuscleX@Admin#2026!"` (a concrete credential, not a placeholder). ensureSuperAdmin() seeds an AdminRole.SUPER account from this env value on boot: saas-control-center/src/modules/auth/auth.service.ts:50 `const password = this.config.get<string>('SUPER_ADMIN_PASSWORD');` then `password_hash: await bcrypt.hash(password, SALT_ROUNDS)`.
impact: Unlike other secrets which ship as `<generate-...>` placeholders, this ships a real, guessable value. An operator who copies .env.example to .env (common) provisions the SCC super-admin with a publicly-known password committed to git, granting full control-center access across all tenants.
fix: Replace the value with a placeholder (e.g. `<set-a-strong-unique-password>`) like the JWT secrets in the same file, and document that boot must fail or force a rotation if the default is detected.

verdict.reasoning: Independently reproduced from real code. saas-control-center/.env.example line 26 ships a concrete, guessable credential SUPER_ADMIN_PASSWORD="MuscleX@Admin#2026!" (not a placeholder, unlike JWT_SECRET/JWT_REFRESH_SECRET on lines 13/15 which use `<generate-...>`). Confirmed the file is git-tracked and not gitignored. auth.service.ts ensureSuperAdmin() (lines 48-64), invoked on onModuleInit, reads SUPER_ADMIN_PASSWORD (line 50) and, when no admin with the configured email exists, creates an AdminRole.SUPER account hashing that password (line 59). No boot-time guard rejects the default and no forced rotation exists. SUPER_ADMIN_EMAIL is also a concrete value (line 25), so both credential halves are committed. An operator copying .env.example to .env verbatim provisions a super-admin with a publicly-known password granting cross-tenant control-center access. Severity low is correct because exploitation is contingent on operator negligence (unchanged copy, MFA not enabled) rather than an active runtime flaw.

title: Cross-tenant IDOR: gym owner can credit/debit ANY studio's referral wallet with an unbounded amount
evidence: Class is gated `@Roles('owner', 'super_admin')` (line 41). Endpoint: `manualAdjustment(@Body() dto: ManualAdjustmentDto, @CurrentUser() user)` → `this.admin.manualWalletAdjustment({ studioId: dto.studio_id, amount: dto.amount, ... adminId: user.user_id })` (lines 390-395). The DTO (admin-actions.dto.ts:62-68) binds `studio_id` to any `@IsUUID()` and `amount` to a bare `@IsNumber()` with NO `@Min`/`@Max`. referral-admin.service.ts:240-274 uses `params.studioId` directly — no check that it equals `user.studio_id`.
impact: A regular gym owner (tenant) can pass an arbitrary `studio_id` and any `amount` to credit their own B2B referral wallet with unlimited value (redeemable against subscription = free money) or debit/drain a competitor gym's wallet. Full cross-tenant financial manipulation from a self-serve owner JWT.
fix: Restrict the wallet mutation endpoints to `@Roles('super_admin')` only (this is a platform-admin action, mirrored by the internal SCC endpoint), OR bind `studioId` to `user.studio_id` and reject mismatches. Add `@Min`/`@Max` bounds on `amount` in ManualAdjustmentDto.

verdict.reasoning: Independently reproduced from real code. The controller ReferralsAdminController is gated @Roles('owner', 'super_admin') (referrals-admin.controller.ts:40-41), and 'owner' is the self-serve role auto-assigned to every gym owner at onboarding (auth.service.ts:386/425/788/862/900/1446/1487 etc.); RolesGuard (roles.guard.ts:32,45-47) explicitly admits it. The manualAdjustment handler (lines 384-397) forwards dto.studio_id verbatim to admin.manualWalletAdjustment with NO check that it equals user.studio_id. ManualAdjustmentDto (admin-actions.dto.ts:62-68) binds studio_id to a bare @IsUUID() (any studio) and amount to a bare @IsNumber() with no @Min/@Max. referral-admin.service.ts:240-275 routes positive amount → wallet.credit and negative → wallet.debit on the attacker-supplied studioId. referral-wallet.service.ts:36-42/58-102 keys the wallet purely by studio_id via this.pub (public-schema client), so any studio's wallet can be created/credited/debited. The Prisma $use gym_id injection does not mitigate this: studio_id is an explicit write value on a platform-level (this.pub) model, not a tenant where-clause filter. Result: a paying gym owner can credit their own referral wallet with unbounded value (redeemable against subscription) or drain a competitor's wallet — full cross-tenant financial IDOR from a self-serve owner JWT. No compensating control found (no ownership check, no amount bounds, RLS is decorative per CLAUDE.md). Severity critical is appropriate.

title: Cross-tenant read/freeze of another studio's referral wallet by a gym owner
evidence: On the same `@Roles('owner','super_admin')` controller: `getWallet(@Param('studio_id', ParseUUIDPipe) studioId)` returns `this.wallet.getBalance(studioId)` + `listEntries(studioId,{limit:50})` (lines 350-355); `freezeWallet` (358-370) and `unfreezeWallet` (372-382) likewise act on the `:studio_id` path param with no binding to `user.studio_id`.
impact: Any gym owner can read another gym's referral wallet balance and last 50 ledger entries, and freeze/unfreeze a competitor's wallet — cross-tenant data disclosure and denial of a paid feature.
fix: Same as above: scope these to `super_admin`, or assert the path `studio_id` matches the caller's `user.studio_id`.

verdict.reasoning: Independently reproduced. The controller api/v1/admin/referrals is class-guarded with @Roles('owner','super_admin') (referrals-admin.controller.ts:41). 'owner' is a per-gym tenant role: RolesGuard (roles.guard.ts:44-47) bypasses on user.role==='owner', the JwtPayload carries studio_id (current-user.decorator.ts:51), and branch-scope.util.ts:19 documents 'owner' as a single-studio gym-wide role. The wallet endpoints (lines 349-382) take the :studio_id path param (and manualAdjustment takes dto.studio_id) with NO comparison to user.studio_id. The service layer confirms no compensating control: ReferralWalletService.getBalance/listEntries (referral-wallet.service.ts:44,272) and ReferralAdminService.freezeWallet/unfreezeWallet (referral-admin.service.ts:218,231) operate on the raw studioId against the public schema via PublicPrismaService, so the tenant gym_id auto-injection does not apply. A gym owner using their own JWT can therefore read any other studio's referral wallet balance + last 50 ledger entries and freeze/unfreeze a competitor's wallet. Genuine cross-tenant IDOR; the cited evidence is accurate.

title: Inline object-typed @Body() params bypass the global ValidationPipe entirely (no whitelist/type enforcement)
evidence: `@Body() body: { role_name: string; branch_id?: string; permission_overrides?: { grants?: string[]; denials?: string[] } }` — an inline TS type, not a decorated DTO class. NestJS ValidationPipe skips validation when the metatype is `Object`, so `whitelist`+`forbidNonWhitelisted`+`transform` (main.ts:61-65) do not run; `role_name`, `grants[]`, `denials[]` reach `inviteService.createInvite` completely unvalidated. Same pattern in subscription.controller.ts:210/236/379, dashboard-actions.controller.ts:64/85/121, referrals-internal.controller.ts:144.
impact: These bodies receive zero server-side type/shape/length validation despite the app's stated reliance on the global whitelist. An owner can inject arbitrary permission-override strings and role names into staff invites; other endpoints accept unbounded/untyped fields. No mass-assignment leak (services pick fields explicitly), but the validation guarantee assumed elsewhere is absent here.
fix: Replace every inline `@Body()` object literal type with a class-validator DTO class (e.g. SendStaffInviteDto with `@IsIn(validRoles)` on role_name and `@IsString({each:true})` on grants/denials). Only decorated DTO classes are validated/whitelisted.

verdict.reasoning:
The core technical claim is independently reproducible and correct. main.ts:60-66 configures the global ValidationPipe with whitelist+forbidNonWhitelisted+transform. staff.controller.ts:323 declares `@Body() body: { role_name: string; branch_id?: string; permission_overrides?: {...} }` as an inline TypeScript object type, not a decorated DTO class. Inline TS types emit no runtime metadata, so `design:paramtypes` reflection resolves the parameter metatype to `Object`, and NestJS ValidationPipe.toValidate() returns false for `Object` (it sits in the native skip-list String/Boolean/Number/Array/Object). Consequently none of whitelist/forbidNonWhitelisted/transform execute on this body — the validation guarantee the app relies on elsewhere is genuinely absent here. The body flows straight into inviteService.createInvite unvalidated. That defect is real and provable from the code.

However, the finding overstates impact. (1) role_name is NOT actually accepted arbitrarily: staff-invite.service.ts:53-55 rejects unknown roles with `if (!ENTERPRISE_ROLES[params.role_name]) throw new BadRequestException`. (2) The endpoint is gated by @Roles('owner','brand_owner') + @Permissions({module:'staff',action:'create'}) — only the tenant's highest-privilege principal can reach it, and permission-override codes are within that owner's legitimate authority to assign anyway; unknown codes match no real permission and grant nothing. (3) No cross-tenant isolation impact, and the finding itself concedes there is no mass-assignment because services pick fields explicitly. So this is a legitimate defense-in-depth / validation-consistency gap, not a medium-severity exploitable hole.

title: Stale pre-truncate backup schemas retain real member/identity PII in the production DB
file: database state (no schema file): schemas zzz_backup_pre_truncate_20260614, zzz_backup_pre_truncate_20260623
evidence: get_advisors(performance) reports 220 no_primary_key findings, ALL in backup schemas: 200 in zzz_backup_pre_truncate_20260614 and 20 in zzz_backup_pre_truncate_20260623. These are full flat copies of tenant tables: verified row counts zzz_backup_pre_truncate_20260614.public__user_identities = 9 rows and zzz_backup_pre_truncate_20260614.studio_template__members = 115 rows; other copied tables include public__invoices, public__pending_registrations, studio_template__members, studio_template__member_profiles, etc.
impact: Production database holds duplicated, un-tenant-scoped (single flat table, no gym_id RLS parity), un-PK'd copies of sensitive data — identities (2FA-secret/encrypted-password bearing user_identities), member PII, invoices. They persist indefinitely, widen the breach blast radius, and bypass the gym_id isolation model since every gym's members sit in one table. Also a data-governance/GDPR retention issue.
fix: After confirming they are no longer needed, drop the zzz_backup_pre_truncate_* schemas (HARD-STOP: destructive DB op — requires explicit confirmation). If retention is required, move them out of the live prod DB to cold storage. Do not leave production PII in ad-hoc backup schemas.

verdict.reasoning: Independently reproduced against the live DB. Both schemas exist (zzz_backup_pre_truncate_20260614, zzz_backup_pre_truncate_20260623). They contain flat copies of identity/PII/financial tables (public__user_identities, studio_template__members, studio_template__member_profiles, public__invoices, public__pending_registrations) plus an auth_users_snapshot. Row counts match the finding exactly (user_identities=9, members=115). public__user_identities includes secret columns two_factor_secret and two_factor_backup_codes alongside email/phone/full_name; the auth_users_snapshot carries encrypted-password material. All backup tables verified with has_pk=false and rls_enabled=false. Two imprecisions in the writeup, neither fatal: (1) user_identities has no password column itself (auth passwords live in Supabase auth.users, captured separately by auth_users_snapshot), so "encrypted-password bearing" applies via the snapshot, not that table; (2) the "bypass the gym_id isolation model" framing overstates it as an app-layer leak — these schemas are not Prisma-mapped and unreachable through any API route, so there is no runtime cross-tenant leak. The genuine, verified issue is data-at-rest: stale, indefinitely-retained backup schemas holding secret-bearing member/identity PII in the production DB with no PK and no RLS parity, readable by the app's rolbypassrls superuser — widening breach blast radius and creating a GDPR retention problem. This is a real governance/operational-security defect, not a code-path bug.

title: 18 scc.* tables have RLS disabled with zero policies (mitigated: scc not anon-reachable)
file: database state: schema scc; no ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY / CREATE POLICY exists in saas-control-center migrations
evidence: pg_class shows relrowsecurity=false and 0 policies for all 18 scc tables: admin_users, audit_logs, discounts, error_activity_logs, error_occurrences, feature_flags, idempotency_keys, password_reset_tokens, payments, plan_feature_flags, platform_settings, release_tracking, subscription_plans, subscriptions, system_alerts, system_errors, tenant_feature_flags, tenants. Grep of saas-control-center for 'ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY|CREATE POLICY' = No files found (SCC hand-SQL never enables RLS). MITIGATION VERIFIED: has_schema_privilege('anon','scc','USAGE')=false and same for 'authenticated' — so PostgREST anon/authenticated cannot reach scc regardless of RLS.
impact: Low as-is: these tables (super-admin credentials, tenant billing, payments) are only reachable by the backend superuser role, not by the public PostgREST anon/authenticated roles, because the scc schema grants no USAGE to those roles and is not in the exposed-schemas surface. The exposure would become real only if scc were ever added to PostgREST Exposed Schemas or granted to anon/authenticated. NOTE: I could not directly read the PostgREST 'Exposed schemas' config value from the DB; reachability was verified via the schema-USAGE grant, which is the effective gate.
fix: Defense-in-depth: enable RLS on scc.* (deny-by-default) so an accidental future GRANT/expose cannot leak super-admin/billing data. Add a guard test asserting anon/authenticated have no USAGE on scc.

verdict.reasoning: Every technical claim independently reproduced. (1) A pg_class/pg_policy query confirms all 18 scc tables have relrowsecurity=false and 0 policies, matching the finding's table list exactly. (2) Grep of saas-control-center for 'ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY|CREATE POLICY|ROW LEVEL SECURITY' returns no matches — SCC hand-SQL migrations never enable RLS; the only 'anon|authenticated' hits are JWT-role strings in app TypeScript, not Postgres GRANTs. (3) The stated mitigation is real: has_schema_privilege('anon','scc','USAGE')=false and has_schema_privilege('authenticated','scc','USAGE')=false, so PostgREST public roles cannot reach the scc schema regardless of RLS. This is a genuine defense-in-depth gap (no deny-by-default on sensitive super-admin/billing/payments tables) but not an exploitable leak in the current configuration, since the schema-USAGE grant — the effective gate — blocks anon/authenticated access. Severity 'low' is accurate and honestly self-mitigated; the exposure would only become real if scc were added to PostgREST Exposed Schemas or granted USAGE to public roles.

title: anon still holds SELECT/INSERT/DELETE on sensitive public tables; only RLS-with-no-policy prevents the leak
file: database state: public.user_identities, public.user_sessions, public.studios, public.invoices, public.pending_registrations, public.subscription_plans
evidence: anon has schema USAGE on public (verified true). has_table_privilege('anon', ...,'SELECT'/'INSERT'/'DELETE') = true for public.user_identities, user_sessions, studios, invoices, pending_registrations, subscription_plans. These tables have relrowsecurity=true but policy_count=0, so a non-owner role currently sees zero rows (fail-closed). No leak today.
impact: The only thing stopping anon from reading user_identities (2FA secrets, encrypted passwords), user_sessions (token_hash), studios and invoices via PostgREST is that RLS is enabled with no permissive policy. If anyone ever ALTER TABLE ... DISABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY or adds a permissive anon policy, it becomes an instant full-table leak. The leftover table-level GRANTs to anon are a latent footgun (Phase 8.1 revoke did not cover these).
fix: REVOKE ALL ON these public tables FROM anon, authenticated (backend uses the bypass superuser, not these roles) so the grant no longer exists as a single point of failure. Keep RLS enabled as belt-and-suspenders.

verdict.reasoning: All factual claims independently reproduced against the live DB. anon has schema USAGE on public (true); all six tables (user_identities, user_sessions, studios, invoices, pending_registrations, subscription_plans) have relrowsecurity=true with policy_count=0; anon has SELECT/INSERT/DELETE=true on all six; authenticated also has these grants. Sensitive columns confirmed: user_identities.two_factor_secret + two_factor_backup_codes, user_sessions.token_hash. The finding is correct that there is NO active leak today — RLS enabled with zero permissive policies is fail-closed, so anon/authenticated see zero rows through PostgREST. This is a genuine defense-in-depth / latent-risk finding, not a live vulnerability: the leftover table-level GRANTs to anon (which the backend never uses, since it connects as the rolbypassrls superuser) are a single point of failure — disabling RLS or adding one permissive policy would instantly expose 2FA secrets and session token hashes. The Phase 8.1 revoke did not cover these grants. The self-assigned 'low' severity is accurate given no exploitable path exists today.

title: Four unindexed foreign keys on hot public tables
evidence: get_advisors(performance) unindexed_foreign_keys: public.login_history.login_history_device_id_fkey (device_id), public.user_sessions.user_sessions_device_id_fkey (device_id), public.referral_fraud_signals.referral_fraud_signals_referral_id_fkey, public.reward_logs.reward_logs_rule_id_fkey. Confirmed in schema: LoginHistory declares @@index on user_id/email/ip_address/status but none on device_id (schema.prisma:646-649); UserSession indexes user_id/token_hash/expires_at but not device_id (:671-673).
impact: Cascades/joins/deletes on user_devices (e.g. revoking a device, ON DELETE SetNull) and on referral rule/referral lookups do sequential scans of these tables. Minor now (low volume) but grows with login_history/user_sessions size.
fix: Add @@index([device_id]) to LoginHistory and UserSession, and covering indexes for referral_fraud_signals.referral_id and reward_logs.rule_id.

verdict.reasoning: All four unindexed foreign keys independently verified from backend/prisma/schema.prisma: (1) LoginHistory.device_id — FK to UserDevice with onDelete:SetNull (line 644), indexes at 646-649 cover only user_id/email/ip_address/status, no device_id index. (2) UserSession.device_id — FK with onDelete:SetNull (line 669), indexes 671-673 cover user_id/token_hash/expires_at, no device_id index. (3) ReferralFraudSignal.referral_id — FK (line 4519), indexes 4522-4523 cover review_status+severity and subject_studio_id, no referral_id index. (4) RewardLog.rule_id — FK (line 4477), indexes 4480-4482 cover beneficiary_studio_id+status, referral_id, applied_at, but NOT rule_id. The finding correctly distinguishes indexed vs unindexed columns (notably reward_logs.referral_id IS indexed but rule_id is not — matching the advisor's rule_id flag). Genuine low-severity performance issue: FK-parent deletes and joins do sequential scans; impact minor now, grows with table size.

title: 1481 unused indexes and RLS-initplan / multiple-permissive-policy perf warnings (informational)
evidence: get_advisors(performance) lint counts: unused_index=1481, auth_rls_initplan=147 (WARN), multiple_permissive_policies=20 (WARN, e.g. studio_template.domain_events has both `gym_isolation` and `tenant_isolation` permissive policies for the same role/action). unused_index is INFO-level and expected because most studio_template tables are still empty pre-launch, so indexes have no scans yet.
impact: Unused-index count is not actionable now (empty tables); do not drop indexes based on it pre-launch. The auth_rls_initplan warnings (per-row re-eval of auth.*/current_setting in RLS USING clauses) and duplicate permissive policies add query overhead on studio_template, but RLS is currently decorative (backend runs as rolbypassrls superuser) so the runtime cost is not paid on the hot path today. Becomes relevant only when the non-bypass RLS keystone ships.
fix: No action pre-launch. When the RLS keystone lands, wrap auth/current_setting calls as (SELECT ...) to hoist them to initplan, and collapse the duplicate gym_isolation/tenant_isolation policies into one per table/action. Re-run the linter against populated tables before pruning any index.

verdict.reasoning: I independently reran get_advisors(performance) and every cited count matches exactly: unused_index=1481 (INFO), auth_rls_initplan=147 (WARN), multiple_permissive_policies=20 (WARN). The specific example is also verified — studio_template.domain_events carries both `gym_isolation` and `tenant_isolation` permissive policies for the same role/action (reproduced across anon/authenticated/authenticator/dashboard_user/supabase_privileged_role for all four DML actions). The impact analysis is consistent with the codebase's documented ground truth: RLS is decorative because the backend connects as a rolbypassrls superuser, so the initplan re-eval and duplicate-policy overhead are not paid on the current hot path; the unused_index count is expected because most studio_template tables are empty pre-launch (corroborated by no_primary_key=220, indicating scaffolding-stage tables). The finding is accurately measured and correctly self-classified as informational, with sound guidance (no action pre-launch; hoist auth/current_setting into (SELECT ...), collapse duplicate policies, and re-lint against populated tables before pruning indexes). This is a real, verifiable database-state observation, not a code defect and not fabricated — severity info is appropriate since nothing is exploitable or currently broken.

title: Staff access AND refresh tokens persisted in localStorage — any XSS = full session/account takeover
evidence: persist config: `name: 'auth-storage'` (zustand default = localStorage) with `partialize: (state) => ({ user: state.user, studio: state.studio, accessToken: state.accessToken, refreshToken: state.refreshToken, ... })`. Confirmed read side in frontend/src/services/api-client.ts:65 `const stored = localStorage.getItem('auth-storage');` returning `parsed?.state?.accessToken` and `parsed?.state?.refreshToken`.
impact: Both the staff JWT and the long-lived refresh_token are stored in JS-readable localStorage. Any XSS on the admin app (an app that moves real money and multi-tenant member data) can exfiltrate the refresh token and mint fresh access tokens for a 7-day window (api-client.ts:147 sets max-age 7 days), fully impersonating an owner/brand_owner. A refresh token in localStorage cannot be protected by httpOnly and survives token rotation.
fix: Move the session to an httpOnly, Secure, SameSite=Strict cookie set by the backend/auth-callback route and stop persisting accessToken/refreshToken in the zustand localStorage store. At minimum keep the refresh_token out of JS-reachable storage (httpOnly cookie) and hold only a short-lived access token in memory.

verdict.reasoning: Independently reproduced from the real code. In frontend/src/stores/auth-store.ts the zustand persist config (lines 146-160) uses name: 'auth-storage' with NO custom `storage` option — zustand's persist middleware defaults to window.localStorage — and its partialize (lines 148-155) explicitly persists BOTH `accessToken` and `refreshToken`. The read side in frontend/src/services/api-client.ts:63-76 (getAuthState) does `localStorage.getItem('auth-storage')` and returns `parsed?.state?.accessToken`/`refreshToken`, confirming both tokens sit in JS-readable localStorage. refreshAccessToken (lines 132-154) POSTs that refresh token to /auth/refresh to mint new access tokens, and line 147 sets a 7-day (max-age=60*60*24*7) auth cookie. localStorage is not httpOnly-protectable, so any XSS on the admin app can exfiltrate the long-lived refresh token and continuously re-mint access tokens, fully impersonating an owner/brand_owner. No mitigating control refutes this: the finding's evidence is accurate and not misread, the code path is the live one used by every API call, and there is no separate httpOnly-cookie session mechanism. The only caveat is that exploitation requires a separate XSS foothold, making it a (well-recognized) defense-in-depth weakness rather than an independently-triggerable bug.

title: No Content-Security-Policy header — nothing constrains injected script, compounding localStorage token theft
evidence: setSecurityHeaders() sets only `X-Content-Type-Options`, `X-Frame-Options`, `Referrer-Policy`, and `Permissions-Policy` (lines 53-67). No `Content-Security-Policy` is set here or anywhere (grep for 'Content-Security-Policy' across frontend/ returns no matches).
impact: With session tokens sitting in localStorage/JS-readable cookies (findings above), the absence of any CSP means an injected inline script or a malicious third-party script can freely read those tokens and exfiltrate them to an attacker host. CSP is the primary mitigation that would blunt an XSS-to-token-theft chain.
fix: Add a strict Content-Security-Policy (script-src 'self' with nonces/hashes, connect-src limited to the API + Supabase + Sentry origins, object-src 'none', base-uri 'self') in middleware.ts setSecurityHeaders or next.config headers.

verdict.reasoning: Independently reproduced. frontend/src/middleware.ts setSecurityHeaders() (lines 52-67) sets only X-Content-Type-Options, X-Frame-Options, Referrer-Policy, and Permissions-Policy — no Content-Security-Policy. Grep for 'Content-Security-Policy' across frontend/ returns no matches, and next.config.mjs sets no headers (its own comment states security headers are owned by middleware.ts), so no CSP exists anywhere. The compounding premise is also verified: the auth token is stored JS-readably — localStorage 'auth-storage' (api-client.ts:86) plus a client-set, therefore non-httpOnly, 'auth-token' cookie (api-client.ts:147, auth-store.ts:68) readable via document.cookie. Thus no CSP constrains injected script that could read and exfiltrate those tokens. The code facts in the finding are all accurate; nothing refutes it. Note this is a defense-in-depth gap: it is not independently exploitable and only becomes material if a separate XSS injection vector exists, which lowers the practical severity from medium to low.

title: Route-protection middleware only checks cookie presence, not JWT validity — client-side-only gate
evidence: `const authCookie = request.cookies.get("auth-token"); if (!authCookie?.value) { ... redirect('/login') }` — any non-empty value passes; the JWT signature/expiry is never verified.
impact: Setting `document.cookie='auth-token=x'` bypasses the SSR route guard and renders the authenticated shell. This is not a data leak on its own — the backend API remains authoritative and every data fetch carries the real Bearer JWT (api-client.ts:255) — but the middleware provides a false sense of gating and would serve the app shell to an unauthenticated visitor.
fix: Either verify the JWT (signature + exp) in middleware, or treat middleware purely as UX and never rely on it for authorization (which the current backend design already does). Prefer verifying so the shell isn't served to forged cookies.

verdict.reasoning: Independently reproduced from frontend/src/middleware.ts. Line 38 reads `const authCookie = request.cookies.get("auth-token");` and line 40 gates only on `if (!authCookie?.value)`. There is no JWT signature or expiry verification anywhere in the file — any non-empty cookie value passes the guard and the authenticated shell is served. A forged `document.cookie='auth-token=x'` bypasses the SSR route guard. The finding is technically correct and, importantly, honestly scoped: it explicitly acknowledges this is NOT a data leak because the backend API remains authoritative (every data fetch carries a real Bearer JWT that the backend validates), so the practical impact is limited to serving the app shell / false sense of gating. This is a genuine defect but correctly rated low severity — the middleware is soft-authz UX, not a security boundary, and no sensitive data is exposed by the client-side render alone.

title: Dev OTP login bypass gated only on NODE_ENV, accepts any 4–8 digit code — full member account takeover in any non-prod env against the shared DB
evidence: private get devBypassEnabled(): boolean { return this.config.get<string>('NODE_ENV') !== 'production'; }  ...  const ok = fixed ? entered === fixed : /^\d{4,8}$/.test(entered); if (!ok) throw MemberException.invalidToken('Invalid dev code.'); ... const appUser = await this.appUsers.findOrCreate(normalized); ... return this.sessionForAppUser(appUser.id, normalized, tenantId);
impact: The POST /member/v1/auth/dev/session route (member-auth.controller.ts:49) issues REAL member tokens for any phone number with NO SMS/OTP. The controller comment (line 46-47) claims it '404s unless ... non-production + MEMBER_DEV_OTP set', but the implementation only checks NODE_ENV !== 'production' and, when MEMBER_DEV_OTP is unset, accepts ANY 4–8 digit code. Per CLAUDE.md all four apps share ONE production Supabase Postgres DB, so any staging/preview/dev backend pointed at that DB with NODE_ENV != 'production' lets anyone who knows a real member's phone number log in as that member (sessionForAppUser resolves their gym scope) — full account takeover of gym-scoped member data. The account's safety rests entirely on NODE_ENV being set to exactly 'production' everywhere touching prod data, and the documented second factor (MEMBER_DEV_OTP) is not actually required.
fix: Require BOTH NODE_ENV !== 'production' AND a configured MEMBER_DEV_OTP (i.e. return devBypassEnabled only when fixedDevOtp is non-null), matching the controller's documented contract; never accept an arbitrary well-formed code. Consider an additional explicit MEMBER_DEV_BYPASS=true flag so a mis-set NODE_ENV alone cannot enable it.

verdict.reasoning: Every technical claim is independently reproduced from the real code. member-auth.service.ts:49-51 gates the dev bypass solely on NODE_ENV !== 'production'. fixedDevOtp (lines 58-61) is null when MEMBER_DEV_OTP is unset, and line 114 (`const ok = fixed ? entered === fixed : /^\d{4,8}$/.test(entered)`) then accepts ANY 4–8 digit code. devSession (lines 117-127) proceeds to findOrCreate the app_user and sessionForAppUser resolves gym scope by phone, so knowing a real member's phone yields a gym-scoped member token with no SMS/OTP. The controller docstring (member-auth.controller.ts:46-47) and DTO docstring (auth.dto.ts:46-48) both assert the route requires "non-production + MEMBER_DEV_OTP set," but the implementation never enforces MEMBER_DEV_OTP — a real documentation/implementation drift that gives a false sense of a second factor. The controller is registered unconditionally (member.module.ts:79); the NODE_ENV check inside devSession is the only gate. Refutation attempts (conditional module registration, additional guard, stricter DTO validation) all failed. Given CLAUDE.md/memory ground truth that all environments share one production Supabase DB, any non-prod backend (NODE_ENV != 'production') pointed at that DB enables full member account takeover. The primary prod backend runs NODE_ENV=production and correctly 404s, so exploitation is conditional on a misconfigured/staging deployment against the shared DB rather than the main prod host — which is why I keep it high but not critical.

title: SCC member-app analytics/CRM/campaign endpoints have no @Roles gate — any admin role reaches all-app-user data and can blast push campaigns
evidence: /** All routes are super-admin (global) — protected by the app-wide JwtAuthGuard. */ ... @Controller('member-app') export class MemberAppAnalyticsController {  @Get('leads') ...  @Get('leads/export') ...  @Get('crm') ...  @Post('campaigns/:id/send') ...  @Post('automations/:key/run')  — no @Roles(...) on the class or any handler.
impact: RolesGuard treats a handler with no @Roles as 'any authenticated admin passes' (roles.guard.ts:36). AdminRole includes SUPER, BILLING, SUPPORT (schema.prisma:39). The class comment asserts these routes are 'super-admin' but nothing enforces it, so a lower-privileged SUPPORT/BILLING admin can pull the full app-user CRM (name/city/gym/masked-phone of every public user), export the leads CSV, and — more significantly — create and SEND push-notification campaigns and run automations to all members. This is inconsistent with the least-privilege gating applied on tenant.controller.ts and system-errors.controller.ts. (Phone is masked in list/export, limiting PII leakage.)
fix: Add @Roles(AdminRole.SUPER) (or the intended allowlist) at the controller level, mirroring TenantController; at minimum gate the campaign send/automation-run mutations behind SUPER.

verdict.reasoning:
Every claim in the finding reproduces against the real code:

1. No @Roles gate: I read the full controller (saas-control-center/src/modules/member-app-analytics/member-app-analytics.controller.ts). There is no @Roles decorator on the class (line 59-62) or on any of the ~18 handlers, including the sensitive Get('leads'), Get('leads/export'), Get('crm'), Post('campaigns/:id/send') (line 170), Patch('automations/:key'), and Post('automations/:key/run') (line 189). Only the misleading comment at line 57 asserts "All routes are super-admin."

2. Guard fail-open confirmed: roles.guard.ts line 36 — `if (!allowed || allowed.length === 0) return true;` — a handler with no @Roles lets any authenticated admin pass. Comment at line 18/35 states this explicitly ("Routes with NO @Roles() allow any authenticated admin").

3. Guard is actually active: auth.module.ts lines 27-28 register both JwtAuthGuard and RolesGuard as global APP_GUARDs, so RolesGuard runs on these routes and does fall through to line 36.

4. AdminRole includes lower-privilege roles: prisma/schema.prisma lines 39-43 define enum AdminRole { SUPER, BILLING, SUPPORT }. Guard reads req.user.role (line 39), so a SUPPORT or BILLING admin passes.

5. Inconsistency is real: tenant.controller.ts gates every route with @Roles (e.g. lines 50/77/92 use @Roles(AdminRole.SUPER) for privileged ops); plans, subscription, and system-monitoring controllers also use @Roles. member-app-analytics is an outlier with none, so a SUPPORT/BILLING admin can pull the full CRM, export leads CSV, and — more significantly — create/send push campaigns and run automations to all app users.

The only mitigating factor (also acknowledged in the finding) is that phone numbers are masked in the list/export, limiting PII leakage. Severity low is appropriate: this is an internal super-admin control center where all authenticated principals are trusted staff, so this is a least-privilege / segregation-of-duties gap rather than an external exposure — but it is a real, provable gap, not correct-as-is.

title: Razorpay webhook security gate (HMAC verify + replay window) has no test
evidence: razorpayWebhook() performs the only trust boundary for inbound money events: `const expected = createHmac('sha256', webhookSecret).update(bodyStr).digest('hex');` then `signatureValid = timingSafeEqual(Buffer.from(expected,'hex'), Buffer.from(signature ?? '','hex'))`, plus a 300s replay window `if (eventAge > 300) ... throw new ForbiddenException`. No spec exercises this controller method — razorpay.service.spec.ts only tests `verifyCheckoutSignature` (the checkout handshake, a different code path), and payment-atomic-claim.spec.ts only tests the downstream `handleRazorpayWebhook` service method AFTER the gate. Grep for 'razorpayWebhook'/'created_at'/'replay' in backend/test returns no hit against this endpoint.
impact: A regression that weakens signature comparison, breaks the rawBody path (`bodyStr = rawBody ? rawBody.toString('utf8') : JSON.stringify(req.body)` — the fallback re-serializes and would not match Razorpay's signature), or removes the replay window would let a forged/replayed payment.captured event mark invoices paid, and CI would stay green. This is the single un-regression-tested security gate on the payment ingress.
fix: Add a controller-level spec: valid signature accepted; tampered signature -> ForbiddenException; missing secret -> BadRequestException; created_at older than 300s -> ForbiddenException. Assert timingSafeEqual is fed the raw body, not JSON.stringify(req.body).

verdict.reasoning: Independently verified all factual claims. payments.controller.ts:130-180 contains razorpayWebhook() with: HMAC-SHA256 via createHmac (line 146), timingSafeEqual signature check (line 150), BadRequestException on missing secret (line 140), and a 300s replay window throwing ForbiddenException (lines 163-167). The rawBody-vs-JSON.stringify fallback is real (line 145). Grepping backend/test for razorpayWebhook, webhooks/razorpay, x-razorpay-signature, timestamp expired, and Invalid webhook signature returns zero matches — no spec exercises this controller method. razorpay.service.spec.ts covers only verifyCheckoutSignature (a different checkout-handshake path), createOrder, and configured. payment-atomic-claim.spec.ts covers only PaymentsService.handleRazorpayWebhook, the downstream service method invoked after the gate (controller line 175), not the HMAC/replay gate. The finding is accurate: the single trust boundary for inbound money events has no regression test. I downgrade severity from high to medium because the control itself is present and correct today — this is a regression-safety/coverage gap, not a live exploitable vulnerability; there is no proven current exploit path, only the risk that a future change silently weakens the gate with CI staying green.

title: Jest coverage thresholds set very low (branches 20%, statements/lines 30%)
evidence: "coverageThreshold": { "global": { "statements": 30, "branches": 20, "functions": 25, "lines": 30 } }
impact: The gate can pass with 80% of branches (including auth/payment/tenant error paths) unexecuted. New untested critical code does not fail CI as long as global stays above these floors, so the threshold provides almost no protection against coverage erosion on money/isolation paths.
fix: Raise global thresholds incrementally and/or add per-directory thresholds (e.g. src/payments, src/auth, src/prisma, src/subscription) at a materially higher bar than 20-30% so critical modules cannot silently lose coverage.

verdict.reasoning: The cited code is exactly as reported. backend/package.json lines 129-136 read: "coverageThreshold": { "global": { "statements": 30, "branches": 20, "functions": 25, "lines": 30 } }. The evidence quote is verbatim, and the factual claim is accurate: the only threshold is a single low global floor with no per-directory (payments/auth/prisma/subscription) thresholds, so critical modules can lose coverage without failing CI as long as the aggregate stays above these floors. The impact description is technically correct — a branches floor of 20% means up to 80% of branches (including error/auth/tenant paths) can be unexecuted while the gate passes.\n\nHowever, this is a CI/process-hygiene observation, not an actual runtime defect, security bug, or tenant-isolation flaw. It does not itself cause incorrect behavior, a leak, or a crash; it merely provides weak protection against future coverage erosion. There is no failing scenario in the current code — only a weakened guard-rail. Given the audit's mandate to prefer real high-severity defects, the reported "medium" overstates this. It is a legitimate but low-severity hygiene finding.

title: @types/ioredis v4 declared against ioredis v5 runtime (stale/incorrect types)
evidence: runtime dep "ioredis": "^5.10.0" while devDep "@types/ioredis": "^4.28.10". ioredis v5 ships its own bundled types; the standalone @types/ioredis package covers the v4 API and is deprecated for v5.
impact: Type definitions describe the v4 API surface against a v5 runtime, so type-checking can accept calls that differ at runtime or reject valid v5 usage. It also pulls an abandoned DefinitelyTyped package into the tree unnecessarily.
fix: Remove @types/ioredis and rely on ioredis v5's built-in types; run tsc --noEmit to confirm.

verdict.reasoning: The factual core is verifiable from backend/package.json: line 55 declares runtime "ioredis": "^5.10.0" while line 81 declares devDep "@types/ioredis": "^4.28.10". @types/ioredis is the deprecated DefinitelyTyped package covering the v4 API; ioredis v5 bundles its own types. So a stale/unnecessary deprecated type package is genuinely present against a v5 runtime — a real dependency-hygiene issue.\n\nHowever, the finding's stated IMPACT is overstated/refuted. All six consumers use `import Redis from 'ioredis'`, and TypeScript module resolution prefers a package's own bundled declarations (ioredis v5's built-in types, via its package.json types/exports) over @types/*. The bundled v5 types therefore win and drive type-checking; the standalone @types/ioredis is effectively shadowed. It is not actually causing v4 types to be applied to v5 code — so it will not silently accept calls that differ at runtime. The residual problem is only an abandoned, redundant devDependency in the tree. Confirmed as a real but purely cosmetic hygiene nit, not a low-severity type-safety risk; downgraded to info.

title: gym-member-app has zero automated tests (verification is tsc + on-device QA only)
evidence: Glob for *.spec.* / *.test.* under gym-member-app (excluding node_modules) returns nothing, and package.json scripts define start/android/ios but no `test` script. Confirms CLAUDE.md's statement that this app relies on `node_modules/.bin/tsc --noEmit` plus device QA.
impact: All member-app logic (auth token handling, member-BFF API calls, offline/optimistic flows) is unverified by any repeatable check; regressions are only catchable by manual on-device testing, which is not run in CI. Acknowledged/expected per project rules, so flagged as residual risk not a new defect.
fix: At minimum add a jest config for the pure-logic modules (api clients, streak/date utils, confirm helpers) so non-RN-UI logic has regression coverage; keep animation/layout as device QA.

verdict.reasoning: Independently reproduced every factual claim. gym-member-app/package.json (lines 6-17) defines start/android/ios/web/typecheck/lint/gen:api but no `test` script. Glob for *.spec.*/*.test.* under gym-member-app/src returns nothing; the only matches are inside node_modules (third-party libs). No jest.config.* or jest.setup.* exists. So the app has zero repeatable automated coverage — auth token handling, member-BFF API clients, offline/optimistic flows are only checked by tsc --noEmit (types, not behavior) plus manual on-device QA. This is factually correct and a real residual risk. It is not a code-logic bug and is explicitly acknowledged by CLAUDE.md ("gym-member-app has no tests"), so low severity is appropriate rather than a new high-severity defect.
